To do something idolatrously means to do it with extreme, blind, almost god-like worship — an adoration so excessive and uncritical that it loses all proportion and sense.
Start here: what is an idol?

An idol is a physical object — a statue, an image, a figure — that people worship as if it were a god. Throughout history, many religions and cultures had people bowing before stone or wooden statues, offering them gifts, praying to them, and treating them as divine beings.

The problem, as critics of this practice saw it, was that people were giving total, blind devotion to something that was — after all — just stone or wood. Their worship was excessive, irrational, and misdirected.

That core idea — total, unquestioning, excessive devotion — is exactly what the word idolatrously carries, even when used outside a religious context.

In a strictly religious or historical context, idolatrously means: in the manner of someone who worships idols.

The ancient priests idolatrously bowed before the golden statue, burning incense and chanting prayers to it every morning.

Here it simply describes the act of idol worship — literally prostrating before a carved image as though it were a god.
The figurative meaning (how it's used most of the time)

In modern, everyday usage, idolatrously almost never refers to literal idol worship. Instead, it describes the attitude of idol worship — that same blind, excessive, all-consuming devotion — applied to any person, thing, or idea.

Whenever someone admires or follows something/someone with a level of devotion that is:

  • Extreme (far beyond normal admiration)
  • Uncritical (no questioning, no flaws seen)
  • Almost worshipful (as if the object of admiration were a god)

…then they are doing it idolatrously.

She idolatrously followed every word her favorite author wrote, treating each sentence as sacred truth that could never be questioned.

He idolatrously admired the tech billionaire, defending his every decision and hanging his portrait above his desk.

The crowd idolatrously screamed and wept at the singer's feet, as though they were in the presence of a divine being.
The crucial quality: blind, uncritical excess

What separates idolatrously from ordinary words like "admiringly" or "devotedly" is the implication of excess and loss of reason.

  • Admiringly → you appreciate something; healthy, balanced.
  • Devotedly → you are strongly committed; still reasonable.
  • Idolatrously → you worship it beyond all reason; your judgment is gone.

The person who acts idolatrously cannot see flaws. They will not hear criticism. The object of their devotion has been placed so high on a pedestal that it has become, in their mind, perfect and untouchable — like a god.

This is why the word almost always carries a critical or disapproving tone. When a writer uses "idolatrously," they are usually gently (or not so gently) mocking or criticizing the person doing the worshipping — suggesting that their admiration has gone too far.

Fans idolatrously defended the director's worst film, refusing to accept any criticism of it.

The writer here is clearly signaling: these fans have lost their critical sense.

A person can act idolatrously toward:

  • A celebrity or public figure — treating them as flawless and divine
  • A leader or mentor — following their ideas without any independent thought
  • Money or possessions — treating wealth as the highest possible good, something to be "worshipped"
  • An ideology or belief system — following it blindly, without examination
  • A piece of art or literature — refusing to allow any critique of it
  • Even a memory — clinging to the past so intensely that it becomes an obsession

He idolatrously clung to his dead father's old opinions, treating them as commandments that could never be updated or questioned.

• It does not mean simply liking something a lot. You can love a book without being idolatrous about it.
  • It does not mean being religious or spiritual in a healthy, considered way.
  • It does not imply hatred or negativity toward the thing being worshipped — in fact, quite the opposite. The person worshipping is devoted; the word criticizes the manner and degree of that devotion, not the object itself.

Ask yourself: "Has this person's admiration crossed into something irrational, unquestioning, and absolute — where they treat the object of admiration as if it were a god?"

If yes → the word idolatrously fits.

Idolatrously means: in a manner of total, uncritical, excessive worship — the way someone might bow before an idol — applied to any person, idea, or thing. It always implies that the devotion has gone beyond reason, and it almost always carries a subtle criticism of that excess. It is the adverb for admiration that has lost its sense of proportion.
